area_summary:
The bot is small and mostly careful: store writes are atomic, discord.js lookups hit the cache first, WS payloads are capped at 64 KB and REST calls sit inside try/catch. Two problems are serious. First, a single unauthenticated HTTP request crashes the process, because `new URL` in the request listener is not guarded. I reproduced the crash in /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-memedrop/065ca17e-4939-5472-b348-276c03e80469/scratchpad/audit-scratch/url-crash-client.js. Second, every bot deploy leaves all Android clients disconnected: on shutdown the bot sends WebSocket close frames, the OkHttp service ignores onClosing, and its heartbeat cannot recover after that. Switching shutdown to terminate() on the bot side fixes the APKs already installed.

Next in importance:
- Any linked client can drive unbounded Discord REST work: register arrays have no size cap and there is no per-socket message limit.
- The TTS rate limit trusts the first X-Forwarded-For entry, which the client chooses.
- A PC and a phone on the same account permanently unlink each other.
- Concurrent identical TTS requests each go to Google (simulated: /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-memedrop/065ca17e-4939-5472-b348-276c03e80469/scratchpad/audit-scratch/tts-stampede.js), with no upstream timeout.
- The unused GuildMessages intent is the bot's main idle cost.

Checked and not worth changing:
- Promise.all over the REST loops: discord.js runs same-route requests one at a time and lookups are cache-first, so there is no latency gain. Only the cooldown race and the awaits before the first reply matter.
- Timers without unref: this is a long-running server that exits explicitly with process.exit.
- Cooldown, recentDrops and extensionCodes maps: bounded by the number of users, or swept.
- Per-recipient JSON.stringify: negligible; folded into the delivery refactor.
- Unhandled rejections: none found apart from the synchronous URL throw.
- deploy-commands re-registering at boot: the bulk overwrite is idempotent and uses no create quota. It only adds one REST call to startup, and Fly's start command is not in the repo.

Not verifiable here: the Fly config (needs a single always-on machine, a volume for DATA_DIR, the LINK_SECRET secret, and proxy concurrency/idle limits). Also, /unlink cannot revoke a token held by an offline device, because the HMAC tokens never expire.

findings.title: One malformed HTTP request crashes the bot (unguarded new URL in the request listener)
findings.evidence: index.js:95-96 runs `const u = new URL(req.url, 'http://localhost');` unguarded inside the http 'request' listener. Node's HTTP parser accepts request-targets that the WHATWG URL parser rejects, e.g. `GET //localhost:99999/ HTTP/1.1` (port > 65535) or `GET //[ HTTP/1.1`, and a synchronous throw in a 'request' listener is an uncaught exception. Reproduced with a copy of lines 95-108 (Node 22): the process exits with code 1, `TypeError: Invalid URL at new URL`. `//localhost:99999/` contains only path characters, so Fly's proxy should forward it unchanged. One unauthenticated request kills the only bot instance: all overlays drop, delayed drops, pending codes and cooldowns are lost, plus up to 500 ms of debounced store writes.
findings.behavior_change: bugfix: malformed request targets get HTTP 400 instead of crashing the process
findings.risk: None: only requests that currently crash the process take the new branch.
findings.value: Removes an unauthenticated one-request remote crash (DoS) of the single bot instance.

findings.title: Android never reconnects after the bot closes the socket cleanly (i.e. after every bot redeploy)
findings.evidence: Listener (MemeDropService.kt:128-141) overrides onOpen/onMessage/onClosed/onFailure, not onClosing. With OkHttp 4.12 a server close frame only triggers onClosing; onClosed needs the app to call close() itself, and the reader loop stops after the close frame, so the following TCP FIN is never read (no onFailure). The heartbeat (line 46, `Runnable { ws?.cancel() }`) then cancels the call, which invokes no listener once the reader has stopped: onSocketClosed()/scheduleReconnect() never run, `ws` stays set and Hub.status stays "linked". The bot sends a close frame to every client at shutdown (index.js:1254), so after each deploy/restart Android users silently stop receiving drops until they reopen the app and tap reconnect.
findings.behavior_change: bugfix: Android reconnects on its own after a bot restart/redeploy and after a heartbeat timeout
findings.cross_component: bot/index.js shutdown handler (bot-shutdown-close-frames) is the bot-side mitigation for APKs already installed
findings.risk: Low. OkHttp semantics stated from memory (its documented contract: call close() in onClosing to get onClosed), high confidence; not runnable here.
findings.value: Restores automatic recovery for every Android user after each bot deploy or restart.

findings.title: Shutdown sends WebSocket close frames that strand every installed Android APK
findings.evidence: The SIGINT/SIGTERM handler (index.js:1251-1258) does `wss.clients.forEach(ws => ws.close())`, i.e. sends a close frame to every client. APKs up to 1.6.0 ignore onClosing (see android-onclosing-never-reconnects) and never reconnect after receiving one; APK updates are manual (Updater.kt), so these builds will stay in use for a long time. A TCP close without a close frame is already handled by both clients: OkHttp's reader hits EOF → onFailure → reconnect; Electron's ws emits 'close' (1006) → scheduleReconnect (overlay/main.js:498-505). Fly sends the kill signal on every deploy and machine restart.
findings.behavior_change: bugfix: Android clients reconnect by themselves after bot redeploys; Electron behaviour unchanged
findings.risk: Clients see close code 1006 instead of 1005; neither client inspects close codes.
findings.value: Fixes the most visible Android reliability problem for already-installed APKs with a bot-only deploy.

findings.title: Any linked client can trigger unbounded Discord REST work (uncapped register arrays, no per-socket message limit)
findings.evidence: register stores client-supplied guildIds/blockedIds uncapped (362-363; ~3000 IDs fit in 64 KB). buildBlockedSnapshot (285-298) awaits client.users.fetch(id) for every blocked ID on each snapshot (register 394, unlink_guild 416, unblock_user 430, GuildUpdate 509, /block 992, /unblock 1010, /link 767/806); unknown IDs 404 and are never cached, so every snapshot re-requests them. ws.on('message') (347) has no rate limit. With its own valid token (kept in clear in the app config) a client can register 3000 fake IDs then spam unblock_user: each message starts a 3000-request loop on discord.js's /users/:id queue (same-route requests run one at a time) → unbounded backlog/memory, starved lookups, and /link,/block,/unblock (which await the snapshot before replying) miss Discord's 3 s deadline. Token check (372) is a plain `!==`.
findings.proposed_change:
1) register: `const SNOWFLAKE = /^\d{17,20}$/; const ids = (a, max) => (Array.isArray(a) ? a : []).map(String).filter(s => SNOWFLAKE.test(s)).slice(0, max);` then `guildIds = new Set(ids(id.guildIds, 100))`, `blockedUsers = new Set(ids(id.blockedIds, 200))`, and register_failed unless `SNOWFLAKE.test(userId)`.
2) Per-socket budget right after `ws.isAlive = true` (348): `const now = Date.now(); if (now - (ws.rlSince || 0) > 10_000) { ws.rlSince = now; ws.rlCount = 0; } if (++ws.rlCount > 30) return;` (a legit client sends ~1 pong/30 s plus rare clicks).
3) buildBlockedSnapshot: use `client.users.cache.get(id)?.username` first; fetch only IDs never tried and remember failures in a module-level `unknownUserIds` Set (username = id), so repeated snapshots cost no REST.
4) /block, /unblock and the /link extension path: reply first, then `pushLinksUpdate(id).catch(() => {})`.
5) Constant-time token check: `const a = Buffer.from(String(id.token || '')), b = Buffer.from(tokenFor(userId)); if (a.length !== b.length || !crypto.timingSafeEqual(a, b))` → register_failed.
findings.behavior_change: none for legitimate clients (limits far above real usage)
findings.risk: A user with >200 blocked IDs (unrealistic) would lose the excess; the client re-persists the trimmed list from links_update. Timing-safe compare is hardening only (network timing attack impractical).
findings.value: Closes a cheap DoS vector available to any user who ever linked and bounds REST/memory per socket.

findings.title: TTS per-IP rate limit is keyed on the client-chosen first X-Forwarded-For entry
findings.evidence: index.js:70-71 keys the limit on `String(req.headers['x-forwarded-for'] || req.socket.remoteAddress || '').split(',')[0]`. Proxies append the connecting IP to an incoming X-Forwarded-For, so behind Fly the first entry is whatever the client sent (Fly gives the trusted address in Fly-Client-IP; ~75% sure Fly appends rather than overwrites XFF, Fly-Client-IP is correct either way). A random X-Forwarded-For per request gets a fresh 30/min bucket, so /tts is an unlimited open relay: every miss hits Google with no global or concurrency cap, which can get the Fly egress IP throttled (TTS then fails for all friends), and ttsHits gains one entry per request until the 5-min sweep (39-42).
findings.risk: Without Fly (local dev) the fallback is the last XFF hop or the socket address, as reliable as today.
findings.value: Restores the intended rate limit and protects the shared Google TTS quota every friend depends on.

findings.title: A user's PC and phone unlink each other permanently (one socket per user + identity wipe on 'replaced')
findings.evidence: userLinks keeps one ws per user, so a second device kicks the first: register (383-387) and /link (745-750) send `{type:'unlinked', reason:'replaced'}` to the previous socket, and both clients delete their stored identity on any 'unlinked' (overlay/main.js:485-487, MemeDropService.kt:232-235) and fall back to a pairing code. Installing the APK (README: 'Sur Windows et sur Android') thus silently unlinks the PC for good; re-linking the PC wipes the phone, and so on. /link also restarts the link with only the current guild (758), losing the other servers. Race: register and /link set userLinks then await buildLinksSnapshot (394, 767); if the other device registers meanwhile, the kicked socket still gets 'linked' and steals the user's extension code (257-259).
findings.proposed_change:
Bot-only, protocol unchanged. userLinks: userId → { sockets: Set<ws>, scope, guildIds, blockedUsers }. Helpers `hasOpen(link)` and `sendToUser(userId, obj)` (stringify once, send to every OPEN socket).
- isReachable, /status, /who, /dropall and the /link extension check use hasOpen(link) instead of link.ws.readyState; deliveries and pushLinksUpdate use sendToUser.
- register: if a link with an open socket exists → `sockets.add(ws)`, union guildIds and blockedUsers ('global' if either side is), send 'linked' to ws and links_update to the others; otherwise create it as today. Never send 'unlinked' here.
- /link with a fresh code while linked: add ws and the current guild to the existing link instead of kicking.
- /unlink and unlink_guild→empty: 'unlinked' + reissuePairingCode on every socket, delete the user's extension codes.
- One extension code per user, sent to all its sockets.
- close: `sockets.delete(ws)`; delete the link and extension codes only when no socket is left.
- After each `await buildLinksSnapshot` in register and /link, send 'linked'/issue a code only if `link.sockets.has(ws)`.
findings.behavior_change: visible: PC and phone of the same account stay linked together and both receive that user's drops; devices no longer unlink each other (bug fix)
findings.cross_component: none required; old clients simply never receive reason 'replaced' any more
findings.risk: Moderate refactor touching every link.ws use (isReachable, delivery, /status, /who, /dropall, /link, /unlink, unlink_guild, close). A user with both devices side by side gets each drop twice (intended).
findings.value: Makes the advertised Windows + Android combination usable and removes a silent, permanent unlink.

findings.title: TTS: identical concurrent requests each go to Google, upstream fetch has no timeout, no warm-up
findings.evidence: handleTts fills ttsCache only after the upstream fetch completes (78-86). A /dropall or multi-target /drop with tts makes every overlay request the same URL within ~100 ms; all miss and each calls Google. Simulated with the same logic and a 200 ms mocked upstream: 6 concurrent identical requests → 6 upstream calls (so the comment at 20-21, one Google request per /dropall, is wrong). The fetch has no signal; undici's defaults are 300 s for headers and body, so a stalled Google keeps each overlay's <audio> waiting (its error fallback never fires) for up to 5 min. The upstream call also starts only when the first overlay asks, adding that overlay's fresh HTTPS round-trip to TTS latency.
findings.behavior_change: none (same audio, starts sooner; upstream failure returns 502 after 8 s instead of hanging up to 300 s)
findings.cross_component: none (overlay.js speakTTS already falls back on <audio> error)
findings.risk: A failed upstream call fails all joined requests at once; each overlay falls back exactly as today.
findings.value: One Google request per text instead of one per recipient (less throttling risk), lower TTS latency, bounded hung requests.

findings.title: Unused GuildMessages intent streams, parses and caches every message of every server 24/7
findings.evidence: index.js:497-499 creates the client with `intents: [GatewayIntentBits.Guilds, GatewayIntentBits.GuildMessages]`, but nothing in bot/ listens to message events (no messageCreate or message-cache use). GuildMessages makes Discord push MESSAGE_CREATE/UPDATE/DELETE for every message in every channel the bot can see; discord.js parses each one, builds a Message, caches up to 200 per channel (default MessageManager limit) and adds every author/member to the unbounded user and member caches. Interactions, channels.fetch and ch.send (reaction posts) need none of it. On active friend servers this is the bot's main steady-state CPU, bandwidth and memory cost on the small Fly VM.
findings.proposed_change:
`intents: [GatewayIntentBits.Guilds],`
Optionally also `makeCache: Options.cacheWithLimits({ ...Options.DefaultMakeCacheSettings, MessageManager: 0 })` (add Options to the discord.js import) so the bot's own reaction posts aren't cached either. GuildMessages is not a privileged intent: no Developer Portal change needed.
findings.risk: None known: no code path reads message events or the message cache.
findings.value: Removes the largest idle gateway/CPU/memory load of the bot.

findings.title: Missing LINK_SECRET or volume on Fly fails silently (mass unlink, wiped favorites); prod config undocumented
findings.evidence: Without LINK_SECRET, index.js:205-210 only warns and uses a random secret: after each restart every token is invalid, every client gets register_failed and deletes its identity (main.js:467-470, MemeDropService.kt:216-219), so everyone must /link again, which setting the secret later cannot undo. store.js:16 defaults DATA_DIR to bot/data on the machine's root filesystem, which Fly replaces on deploys/restarts unless a volume is mounted: favorites/groups/stats silently reset. bot/ only carries Railway files (railway.json, nixpacks.toml), .env.example documents neither DATA_DIR nor PUBLIC_BASE_URL, and the Fly config (one always-on machine, volume, secrets) is not in the repo.
findings.proposed_change:
1) After line 205: `if (!process.env.LINK_SECRET && process.env.FLY_APP_NAME) { console.error('[security] LINK_SECRET manquant en production — arrêt (sinon tous les liens seraient invalidés)'); process.exit(1); }` (local dev keeps the ephemeral fallback).
2) Log `[store] DATA_DIR = …` at boot and warn when FLY_APP_NAME is set but DATA_DIR is not.
3) .env.example: add `DATA_DIR=` (must be a Fly volume mount, e.g. /data) and `PUBLIC_BASE_URL=` (optional; FLY_APP_NAME is used otherwise); say PORT comes from the host and DISCORD_TOKEN/CLIENT_ID/LINK_SECRET go in `fly secrets set`.
4) Commit the real config (`fly config save` → bot/fly.toml) and document what this design needs: exactly one machine (`fly scale count 1`; two would split overlays between two bots and handle each interaction twice), auto-stop off (Discord events come over the bot's outbound gateway, nothing would wake a stopped machine), a [[mounts]] volume for DATA_DIR, connection concurrency limits above the number of persistent sockets.
findings.behavior_change: visible: on Fly without LINK_SECRET the bot refuses to start instead of silently invalidating every link
findings.risk: A deploy without the secret now fails loudly (downtime) instead of degrading silently, which is the intent.
findings.value: Prevents an irreversible mass re-link and silent loss of favorites/stats after a host migration or config slip.

findings.title: Clients erase their identity on register_failed, making a transient bot misconfiguration permanent
findings.evidence: overlay/main.js:467-471 (`case 'register_failed': store.set('linkIdentity', null)`) and MemeDropService.kt:216-220 (`Prefs.linkIdentity = null`) delete the stored identity whenever a register is rejected. The bot rejects every valid identity whenever its LINK_SECRET differs from the one that issued the tokens (unset → random secret per boot, or a slip during the Railway→Fly move). Restoring the right secret would make every stored token valid again, but they are already deleted, so every friend must /link again on every device. Keeping a rejected identity costs nothing: the bot re-validates it on every register and the next 'linked' overwrites it.
findings.proposed_change:
Keep the identity on register_failed and just show the pairing code:
- overlay/main.js: `case 'register_failed': setState({ status: 'awaiting_link', code: connState.code || null, user: null, links: null }); break;` (drop the `store.set('linkIdentity', null)`).
- MemeDropService.kt: `"register_failed" -> setState("awaiting_link", Hub.code, null, null)` (drop `Prefs.linkIdentity = null`).
Explicit unlinks still erase it ('unlinked' handlers unchanged). A rejected identity is replayed once per reconnect (one small message) until the user links again or the bot's secret is fixed.
findings.behavior_change: visible: after a rejected register the app keeps its saved link and recovers by itself once the bot's secret is fixed
findings.cross_component: android MemeDropService.kt (same change); bot side: prod-config-silent-failures
findings.risk: Electron briefly shows 'connexion…' on each reconnect before falling back to the code (its pairing_code handler treats a stored identity as a pending re-register).
findings.value: Turns an irreversible mass unlink into a recoverable one.

findings.title: Delayed drops bypass the 2 s cooldown: hundreds of drops can be timed to land in the same minute
findings.evidence: /drop with `delai` (916-933) only consumes the sender's 2 s cooldown when scheduling (908); nothing limits pending delayed drops. Scheduling ~30 drops per minute with decreasing delays (60, 59, 58… min) makes them all fire within the same minute: up to 30 × 60 = 1800 drops (each to up to 5 targets) back-to-back, each possibly with TTS (media-less TTS drops play immediately, bypassing the overlay's queue) or video. Each pending timer also pins its payload and target User objects for up to 60 min.
findings.proposed_change:
```js
const MAX_PENDING_DELAYED = 3;
const pendingDelayed = new Map();   // senderId -> drops différés en attente
```
In /drop read `delai` before markCooldown (908); if `delayMin > 0 && (pendingDelayed.get(uid) || 0) >= MAX_PENDING_DELAYED` → `return safeReply(interaction, "⏳ Tu as déjà 3 drops programmés — attends qu'ils partent.")` without consuming the cooldown. When scheduling: `pendingDelayed.set(uid, (pendingDelayed.get(uid) || 0) + 1)`; first thing in the timer callback: decrement (delete at 0).
findings.behavior_change: visible: a 4th simultaneous delayed drop from the same sender is refused (abuse fix)
findings.value: Keeps the delay feature from defeating the sender cooldown (drop bombs, memory pinned for up to an hour).

findings.title: /dropall and /dropgroup check the cooldown before REST awaits but mark it after (double-submit bypass)
findings.evidence: /dropall checks the cooldown at 945 but marks it at 964, after awaiting `members.fetch(userId)` per candidate (958); /dropgroup checks at 1185, awaits `client.users.fetch` per member (1204), marks at 1210. Fetches are cache-first, but REST happens after each restart and on every call for linked users who left the guild or legacy 'global' links (404 Unknown Member is never cached). During that window a second invocation by the same user passes the check and both deliver. /drop and /dropfav are fine (check and mark are synchronous).
findings.behavior_change: bugfix: the cooldown can no longer be bypassed by double-submitting
findings.value: Small; makes the 15 s /dropall and 2 s /dropgroup limits actually hold.

findings.title: Overlays that re-register before the gateway is READY show 'Aucun serveur' until the next links_update
findings.evidence: The HTTP/WS server listens at module load (493) while client.login runs last (1249). After a restart, an overlay that re-registers before READY gets `links.guilds: []`, because `client.guilds.cache.get(gid)` misses (309-319; the comment at 320-322 notes it). Both settings UIs then show 'Aucun serveur. Utilise /link sur Discord pour en ajouter un.' (overlay/src/settings.js:110-115, android assets/app.js:177-183) although guildIds are intact and drops work; nothing re-sends links_update once guilds arrive. Separately, GuildUpdate (506-512) pushes on any guild change (boosts, settings), making each linked client in that guild re-persist its identity.
findings.behavior_change: bugfix: the linked-servers list displays correctly after a bot restart
findings.cross_component: none (links_update is an existing message both clients handle)
findings.risk: One extra links_update per linked user at boot.
findings.value: Removes a misleading 'run /link again' screen after restarts and needless client writes/wake-ups on unrelated guild updates.

findings.title: store.js: the debounce can postpone writes indefinitely; a corrupt store.json is silently overwritten
findings.evidence: save() (store.js:49-53) clears and re-arms the 500 ms timer on every call, so while saves keep arriving <500 ms apart (bumpStats persists once per recipient, index.js:158-164) nothing is written, and a crash/SIGKILL loses all of it (only SIGINT/SIGTERM flush). Each persistStore() (150-156) also rebuilds the full favorites/groups snapshot although only the last one is written. load() (19-31) treats a JSON parse error like a missing file and returns empty data; the next save then overwrites the unreadable store.json, silently destroying every favorite, group and stat (e.g. after a manual edit).
findings.behavior_change: none (writes at most 500 ms after the first change instead of 500 ms after the last one)
findings.value: Bounded data-loss window on crashes; a corrupt store becomes recoverable instead of silently wiped; less work per drop.

findings.title: Drop delivery is implemented three times (dispatchToTargets, delayed timer, /dropall)
findings.evidence: The canDrop → sendJson → bumpStats → registerDropForReactions sequence exists in dispatchToTargets (643-657), the delayed-drop timer (921-933) and /dropall (967-973). sendJson re-stringifies the same payload per recipient and each bumpStats calls persistStore() (full snapshot rebuild) per recipient. /dropall sends to `r.ws` captured before its awaits (959), so a recipient who reconnected meanwhile is sent to a dead socket. Any delivery change (multi-device sockets, TTS warm-up) has to be made three times.
findings.risk: Low; pure refactor, same messages and stats.
findings.value: One delivery path (needed for multi-device and TTS warm-up), one stringify and one persist per drop.

findings.title: /link codes can be brute-forced: no failure throttle, pending codes never expire
findings.evidence: Pairing codes are 6 digits (231-237) and a pending overlay keeps the same code as long as it stays connected (days for an app left unlinked). /link (735-827) has no attempt limit, so anyone who can run the bot's commands can iterate codes; hitting one of k pending codes links the attacker's account to that victim's overlay, after which the attacker can push any image/video/audio/TTS to it. Expected cost ≈ 1e6/k guesses: slow through Discord, but unthrottled and unbounded in time. Extension codes are bound to their owner (783), so only pending overlays are exposed.
findings.behavior_change: visible: repeated invalid /link attempts are temporarily refused
findings.risk: A user who mistypes 5 times waits up to 10 min.

findings.title: Truncating TTS text by UTF-16 units can split an emoji → URIError → /drop fails
findings.evidence: buildDropPayload truncates with `String(extra.tts).slice(0, MAX_TTS_CHARS)` (589), then ttsUrlFor runs `encodeURIComponent(text)` (585). If the 200-unit cut lands inside a surrogate pair, encodeURIComponent throws: verified in scratch with 'a' + 199×'🔥' (200 code points, 399 UTF-16 units) → 'URIError: URI malformed'. The throw reaches the interaction catch → '⚠️ Internal error' after the cooldown was consumed (908). Reachable only if Discord's max_length counts code points rather than UTF-16 units (likely; not verifiable here). Same slicing at 54 (handleTts → 502 for such input) and 618/1052 (captions → lone surrogate shown as '�').
findings.behavior_change: bugfix: long emoji-heavy TTS text/captions no longer make /drop fail
findings.value: Small; removes an internal-error path for emoji-heavy drops.

findings.title: 30 s application ping wakes every phone 120×/h; ~50 s stays safe for installed clients
findings.evidence: The heartbeat (481-491) sends {type:'ping'} to every client every 30 s and each client answers with a pong: on a phone that is a network wake-up (radio + CPU) every 30 s, 24/7, likely the main idle network cost of the Android service, and the bot dictates it. Both clients only require some message within 75 s (overlay/main.js:363, MemeDropService.kt:34), and those values are baked into installed builds, so the interval can rise to ~50 s without breaking anyone. Trade-off: the bot notices a dead socket after 50-100 s instead of 30-60 s, during which drops to that user are reported as delivered.
findings.proposed_change: `}, 50_000);` at line 491 with `// < 75 s : délai d'expiration codé en dur dans les overlays/APK installés`. Keep the app-level JSON ping (protocol-level ping frames would not re-arm the clients' 75 s timers). Before shipping, check the Fly proxy's idle timeout for WebSockets (fly.toml is not in the repo) and stay below it.
findings.behavior_change: none functionally; dead sockets are detected later (see evidence)
findings.cross_component: none (must stay < 75 s for overlay/main.js and MemeDropService.kt already in the wild)
findings.risk: Medium-low: depends on the proxy idle timeout; slower detection of dead overlays.
findings.value: About 40 % fewer wake-ups for every phone and PC, 24/7.

findings.title: Reconnect backoff has no jitter: all clients retry in lock-step after a bot restart
findings.evidence: scheduleReconnect (overlay/main.js:509-514) and MemeDropService.kt:153-158 use the deterministic `min(30 s, 1000·1.6^attempt)`. Every socket closes at the same instant when the bot stops, so all clients retry at exactly +1.6 s, +4.2 s, +8.3 s, +14.9 s, +25.4 s…: synchronized waves of TLS handshakes and registers (each building a links snapshot) against a bot that is still starting. Harmless at today's scale (tens of clients), cheap to fix.
findings.proposed_change:
Equal jitter, same bounds:
- overlay/main.js: `const base = Math.min(30_000, 1000 * Math.pow(1.6, Math.min(reconnectAttempts, 8)));` then `const delay = base * (0.5 + Math.random() * 0.5);`
- MemeDropService.kt: `val base = minOf(30_000.0, 1000.0 * Math.pow(1.6, minOf(attempts, 8).toDouble()))` then `val delay = (base * (0.5 + Math.random() * 0.5)).toLong()`
findings.value: Low; spreads reconnection bursts after each deploy.
